svg.title: The Boundary Atlas, figure 3: the standard regional cell and the adapter layer
svg.desc: A structural diagram. One standard regional cell is drawn in full and shown stacked, meaning it is stamped per region — identical in form, variant in bindings. Inside the cell, each component names its accountable owner: an issuer plane in its own operator domain, carrying the BL-1 refill contract, owned by the Issuer operator; one or more verification-plane instances, each mapped one-to-one to an accountable verifier domain with its own transactional commit store, independent failure journal, and evidence partition, owned by the regional verifier operator; a trust registry that owns metadata sync and the last-known-good snapshot under freshness policy FP-1, owned by the trust registry operator; an evidence and audit store partitioned per verifier domain with no cross-partition content path of any kind, owned by the regional platform operator; and a supply chain data plane whose residency is governed outside this ledger by the external trade-compliance policy, owned by the data plane owner. Beneath them, an adapter layer is the only layer where a binding product name is load-bearing: five separate kinds of binding — data model, credential format, retrieval protocol, regulatory framework, cryptographic suite — an admission gate returning one of three verdicts, qualified, rejected, or admitted with an explicitly recorded reduced promise, and a versioned manifest whose planned swaps require an overlap window while an emergency retirement disables the binding at once. Below the cell, a dashed federation interface is a sync contract, not a runtime service: anchors, revocation data, and policy activate on local validation under rule 7 and FP-1; only the ledger's epoch is staged and confirmed at both ends; and the coarse BL-1 verdict travels as policy cargo, never as a live callback. No global control plane appears at runtime anywhere in the diagram.
